title: Withdrawal lock
context: Withdrawals run on several app instances. To stop two withdrawals from the same account overlapping, the author added a Redis lock around the balance check and update. The bank payout is an HTTP call.

refs.title: Spring transaction management: @Transactional in depth (Marco Behler)

issues.title: Lock has no expiry
issues.why: If the instance crashes or is redeployed before the delete, the key stays forever and the account can never withdraw again.
issues.fix: Set a lease time when acquiring: setIfAbsent(key, token, Duration.ofSeconds(30)), sized above the worst-case run time.

issues.title: Lock never released on errors
issues.why: The delete only runs on the happy path. Insufficient funds, a bank error or any exception leaves the account locked.
issues.fix: Release the lock in a finally block (or use a helper that always releases).

issues.title: Any instance can release the lock
issues.why: Every holder writes the same value "1". Once a lease expires and another instance takes the lock, the first instance's delete removes the second one's lock.
issues.fix: Store a random token per holder and release with a compare-and-delete Lua script, or use Redisson's RLock.

issues.title: Lock released before the transaction commits
issues.why: The delete runs inside the transaction, before the commit. The next withdrawal can take the lock and read the old balance, so two withdrawals can still overdraw the account.
issues.fix: Lock in the database instead: SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the account row (or a @Version column) gives the same guarantee without Redis.

issues.title: Payout sent inside the transaction
issues.why: If the commit fails after the payout, the money has left but the balance wasn't reduced. A retry pays out twice.
issues.fix: Record the withdrawal as PENDING and commit, then send the payout with an idempotency key (for example through an outbox).

issues.title: Unboxing a nullable Boolean
issues.why: setIfAbsent returns a Boolean that is null inside a Redis pipeline or transaction, so !locked throws a NullPointerException.
